label: Five-star who became a star
title: Five-star who became a star
story: A running back who was one of only 5 seniors at level 96 or higher going into his senior year, he finished high school at 77 overall, started three years at FBS and reached 87. He left after his third season ranked 3rd among draft entrants (grade 85.3) and went 9th overall in round 1. He started from his rookie year, peaked at 93 at 26 and ended every season from 22 to 29 at 90 or better, then declined and was cut after his age-34 season at 73, after 14 pro seasons.
why: Five stars because he really was dominant: only 5 seniors had a level of 96 or higher, well inside the top 100 on film that five stars require, and his upside was real too (potential 91 at the end of high school). Starting all four high school years with above-average coaching (11.3, against an average of 8) helped him grow from 45 at 14 to 77.

He started as a true freshman because college roles rank him only within his own class, and at 77 he was far above the typical five-star's 65. With coaching of 14.3 he reached 87 by 19, and although he slumped at 20 (played like an 82 at 87), his grade of 85.3 was well over the 70 line, so he declared after his third year, the earliest a player can.

Ranked 3rd, he went 9th to a front office of 14 because the 32 teams pick in a random order off their own boards, and each of the eight teams ahead took someone it rated higher, which was luck of the boards. At 87 he started as a rookie. His breakout at 21 (played like a 95) was partly luck, though breakouts are more likely for young starters and competitive hard workers (competitiveness 14, work ethic 12).

He slipped about a point a year from 27 and lost 2 to 4 a year from 30 as ageing set in. Speed goes first (from about 27, moved later by his longevity of +1.5), and backs lean on athleticism. At 34 he ended at 73 and played like a 75, so his team saw about 74 against a cut line of about 77 for a player turning 35 (it rises 1.2 a year past 29): roughly a 1 in 7 chance to stay.

flags.text: He was 77 overall at the end of high school, above the 75 pro starter mark, and 84 after one college season, so college only took him from 77 to 87. Even the best high school backs are not NFL starters at 17. Rawer arrivals (call 1) fix this.

A running back still rated 88 at 30, still starting at 34 (rated 77 going in), and a starter in all 14 pro seasons. Real backs usually fade around 30, but today retirement ignores position and ageing adds no extra wear for backs beyond their speed fading.

label: Five-star bust
title: Five-star bust
story: An interior lineman who was 91 among seniors going into his senior year (81 seniors at or above that level), he signed with FBS as a five-star at 59 overall. He started all four college seasons but never got past 61 and finished at 60 with potential 65. His grade of 58.5 ranked 3,439th, and he was neither drafted nor signed, so he never played as a pro.
why: His five stars rested on an early peak. As an early bloomer (bloom -1.9) he did his growing young, and lucky breakouts at 15 and 16 plus a growth spurt at 16 took him from 38 to 57 in two years, even with poor high school coaching (4.6). That made him 91 among seniors going into his senior year, inside the top 100 on film that five stars need.

Being in the top 100 only makes a player eligible. The star score is 25% film and 75% projected upside, and the scouts' upside guess most likely ran high, because his true ceiling at 17 was 66, only 7 points above his 59.

He started all four years at FBS because college roles rank him only within his own class, yet grew just 1 point (59 to 60). His ceiling was close, and a lost season at 19 cut that year's growth to 40% and dropped his potential from 66 to 63. He also slumped at 21 (played like a 56), and with coachability 7 less of his 13.6 coaching stuck.
He left after four seasons at 60, below the 65 roster mark. His grade of 58.5 ranked 3,439th, and only 257 players are drafted plus about 411 undrafted signings, so no team took him.

flags.text: Most of this bust was set before he signed: at 17 his ceiling was 66, only 7 points above his 59. An early-maturing high school star who stops growing is a real type, but you said five-star busts should start after signing (injury, work ethic, off-field). Should an early bloomer's low ceiling count as one of those reasons? Rawer arrivals (call 1) would make high school dominance say more about early maturity.

label: Dismissed and dropped a level
title: Dismissed and dropped a level
story: A four-star running back who finished high school at 64 and started as a true freshman at FBS. He was dismissed at 19, spent a year starting at FCS, and moved back up to FBS through the portal at 21. He ended every season from 19 to 22 at 66, graded 57.8 (3,834th) with the dismissal on his record, and was neither drafted nor signed.
why: Four stars because he was 89 among seniors going into his senior year (150 at or above that level), about where film alone guarantees four stars (top 150) and well inside the top 1,000 that four stars require. He signed with FBS, drew excellent coaching (17.4) and started at once (64 to 65).

The dismissal was luck, but his work ethic (7) and coachability (5) raised his yearly trouble risk above the 3% base. The year had no games and didn't use one of his four seasons. Dropping to FCS instead of leaving football was also luck, since dismissed players leave 45% of the time.

Still 66 after his FCS year, he was at or above the FBS median, so the portal could move him back up, and unlike most who qualify he chose to go. But he never grew again. A running back leans on athleticism, which is mostly grown by 17 and sooner for an early bloomer (bloom -1.5), his work ethic was low, and he had a lost season at 21 (played like a 62) and stagnation at 22.

His grade of 57.8 includes the 8 points every board takes off for a dismissal and ranked 3,834th, far outside the roughly 668 players drafted or signed. Without it he would have graded about 65.8, still short: in his class a 68.1 grade ranked 637th, near the last players signed.

label: Body stopped growing
title: Body stopped growing
story: A four-star tackle who reached 64 at 17 after two growth spurts, his body stalled (physical ceilings capped for good) in his first FBS season. He crept to 67 by 20, declared early with a grade of 74.6 (94th, round 3) and went 131st in round 4. He spent one season as a rotation player (67 to 68) and was cut at 21.
why: Four stars because he was 90 among seniors going into his senior year (117 at or above that level), likely inside the top 150 on film that guarantees four stars. As an early bloomer (bloom -1.8) he was ahead young (95 among freshmen at 14), and lucky growth spurts at 16 and 17 took him from 54 to 64, with potential 75 at the end of high school.

His body stalled at 18, a chance event that is most likely for early bloomers and caps physical ceilings for good. The same year he slumped (played like a 53 at 64) and his potential slid from 75 to 73, so even with coaching of 14.8 and three years starting he only reached 67, and with coachability 7 less of that coaching stuck.

He declared after his third year because his grade, 74.6, was over the 70 line. His true numbers (67 overall, 74 potential) work out to about 70, so the scouts' read ran nearly 5 points high. Ranked 94th, he slid to 131 because every team picking ahead had someone else higher on its own board, which was luck, and a front office of 11 took him.

At 67 he was a rotation player as a rookie. He ended at 68 but played like a 64, a below-par year by chance, so his team saw about 67 against a line of 68 after round-4 protection: about a 35% chance to stay, and he was cut.

flags.text: A 21-year-old fourth-round tackle rated 68 with potential 74, above the 65 roster mark, was cut after one season, and the cut ended his career. Real teams seldom give up on a day-3 pick that young after one year, and a 68 tackle at 21 would land on a practice squad or another roster.

label: Franchise quarterback
title: Franchise quarterback
story: A five-star quarterback who ended high school at 62 despite very poor coaching (1.2), he started three years at FBS and reached 71. Ranked 37th (grade 78), he went 23rd in round 1, spent two years in a rotation role and started from 23. He peaked at 85 at 30, was still 81 at 35, and retired after 15 seasons.
why: Five stars because he was 91 among seniors going into his senior year (81 at or above that level), inside the top 100 on film, with a big gap between his rating and potential (62 and 82 at the end of high school), which the upside-heavy star score rewards.

He started three years at FBS (coaching 14.8) and grew from 62 to 71. His body stalled at 20, but quarterbacks lean less on athleticism and his potential still rose to 86. A grade of 78, over the 70 line, sent him to the draft after his third year, and it was a fair read: 71 overall and 86 potential work out to about 77 to 78.

Ranked 37th, he went 23rd to a front office of 11, which misjudges by about 3 points, and on that team's board he was the best left. Teams don't value quarterbacks more yet (call 6), so the jump came from that team's misjudgment, which was luck, not his position.

At 71 he began in the rotation and became a starter at 76 at 23, with pro coaching of 13.7. His rating and potential held at 79 and 88 through a major injury at 25, then a lucky breakout at 26 (82, played like an 86) and steady gains took him to a peak of 85 at 30. Still rated 81, he retired at 35 on a chance roll: the yearly chance is past 20% at that age and halved for players rated 78+, roughly 1 in 7.

flags.text: He retired at 35 while still a starter rated 81. Real starting quarterbacks at that level usually play into their late 30s, but retirement odds today ignore position.

label: Quarterback who busted
title: Second-round QB cut while improving
story: A four-star quarterback who rose from 30 at 14 to 63 at 17, he started three years at FBS and reached 69. His grade of 79.5 ranked 22nd, but he slid to pick 51 in round 2. He played two rotation seasons, rising from 69 to 72 with potential 80, and was cut at 22.
why: He climbed from 30 at 14 (74 among freshmen) to 63 by the end of high school, with a lucky breakout at 16 (50 to 60) despite poor coaching (4.8). Going into his senior year he was 93 among seniors (32 at or above that level), inside the top 100 that five stars need, but got four stars. The star score is 75% projected upside and his true ceiling sat only 9 points above his rating (63, potential 72), so most likely the scouts' upside guess wasn't high enough for five.

He started three years at FBS (coaching 16) and declared because his grade, 79.5, was over 70. His true numbers (69 overall, 78 potential) work out to about 72.5, so the scouts' read ran about 7 points high, which is how he ranked 22nd.

Teams pick in a random order off their own boards, and by luck each of the 50 picks before his went to a player that team's board liked more. Then a front office of 7, which misjudges by about 4 points, took him at 51.

He was cut with the odds on his side. After year two he ended at 72 and played like a 70, so his team saw about 71 against a line of 66 after round-2 protection: about a 94% chance to stay. Losing that roll was bad luck, and a weak front office (7) misjudges its own players more than most.

flags.text: A second-round quarterback, 22, rated 72 with potential 80 and still improving, was cut after two seasons despite about a 94% chance to stay, and the cut ended his career. He is one of the 4 to 7 of 64 first- and second-rounders cut within two seasons each class, which is rare in the real NFL.

label: Moved up through the portal
title: Moved up through the portal
story: An unranked running back who was 53 at the end of high school, he signed with a D2 school. A breakout freshman year took him from 53 to 63, he moved up to FBS through the portal at 19, started two years and reached 68. He left with a grade of 72.4 (206th), went 233rd in round 7, and played three rotation seasons at 68 to 70 before being cut at 23.
why: He was well behind at 17. A late bloomer (bloom +2.1) whose growth was still to come, he also had stagnation at 15 and very poor high school coaching (2.2). Going into his senior year he was 73 among seniors (8,259 at or above that level), and he ended high school at 53. FBS passed on him, and FCS and then D2 sign on film, so D2 took him.

As a D2 freshman starter with coaching of 12 (the D2 average is 8.5) he had a breakout year (2.2 times normal growth), 53 to 63. The breakout was partly luck, but as a late bloomer he still had growing to do. At 63 he was at least 2 points above the FBS median, so the portal could move him up, and he was one of the few who chose to go.

Two FBS seasons (coaching 14.4) took him to 68. His grade of 72.4 cleared the 70 line, so he left after his third college year, though his true numbers (68 overall, 71 potential) work out to about 69: the scouts' read ran about 3 points high and tipped him over. Ranked 206th, he went 233rd to a front office of 14.

A seventh-rounder gets no cut protection, and at 68 to 70 he sat right on the line of 70. His chances to stay were about 60%, 46% and 46% after his three seasons, and by luck he survived the first two and lost the third.

flags.text: He left with a year of eligibility left while ranked 206th (round 6), because anyone graded 70 or more after his third year declares. Real players with a late-round grade and a starting job usually stay, more so with NIL money.

label: D2 standout, undrafted
title: D2 standout, undrafted
story: An interior lineman who was 24 overall at 14 and 45 at the end of high school, he signed with a D2 school, redshirted, then started four years and reached 62. His grade of 68.1 ranked 637th, so he went undrafted but signed as an undrafted free agent. He played two seasons as a backup at 62 to 63 and was cut at 24.
why: He started far behind (24 at 14, potential 55) and came on late, as a mild late bloomer (bloom +0.8): after a slump at 15, a lucky breakout at 16 took him from 30 to 41 with good high school coaching (12.8). Going into his senior year he was 71 among seniors (11,675 at or above that level), so FBS and FCS passed and D2 signed him.

He redshirted at 18, as a freshman who would be a backup does, and grew from 45 to 50 that year, helped by the extra physical growth a redshirt year gives. Four years starting and work ethic 13 lifted him to 62 and his potential from 66 to 71, despite D2 coaching of 7.4 and slower skill growth against weaker opponents.

His grade of 68.1 ranked 637th, inside the roughly 668 drafted or signed (257 picks plus about 411 undrafted). His true numbers (62 overall, 71 potential, minus 5 for D2 competition) work out to about 59 to 60, so the scouts' read ran about 8 to 9 points high, and that is what got him a contract.

As a backup he ended year one at 63 and played like a 64, so his team saw about 63 against a line of 70 (undrafted players get no protection): about a 3% chance to stay on those numbers, so staying was luck. After year two (63, played like a 65) the same odds caught him.

flags.text: Rated 62 going into his rookie year, below the 65 roster mark, he still spent a full season on a roster, because every undrafted signing plays a season before the first cut. Most real players like him are cut in camp or land on a practice squad. Camp cuts are part of call 3.

label: Late bloomer
title: Late bloomer
story: An edge rusher who was among the top 2,225 of 250,000 seniors going into his senior year (level 80), he got two stars and signed with FCS. He grew from 54 to 72 over four FCS seasons, including a big final year (65 to 72, college level 85 by its end), and went 60th in round 2. He began in a rotation, started from 24, peaked at 82 at 28, and retired after his age-33 season at 75, after 12 pro seasons.
why: Two stars and FCS: going into his senior year, the season his film comes from, he ranked 2,225th. That is between the top 800, who are guaranteed three stars on film, and the top 3,000, who are guaranteed at least two. So his stars and any FBS offer turned mostly on the scouts' projection of his upside (75% of the star score, 60% of an FBS offer to a two-star). His real potential was 79, so missing both points to a low guess on his upside, which is luck. FCS, which signs on film, took him.

Late growth: bloom +1.2 means he develops like a player 1.2 years younger, and work ethic 15 multiplies his growth by 1.125. After a flat year at 20 (65 to 65, with a moderate injury and a slump) he was still 16 points under his potential of 81, and he gained 7 in his last year with no special event. As a pro he kept adding about 2 a year, reaching the 75 starter mark going into his age-24 season and 80 by 25, even with coaching of 8.6 in his first three seasons.

Draft: his 76.2 grade (1 point off for FCS) ranked 64th, the last spot in round 2 on the consensus board. A front office of 13, whose board strays about 2.75 points, took him 60th, almost exactly where the consensus had him.

End: a major injury at 29 (it takes explosiveness and ceiling) came in the year he dropped from 82 to 80 and his ceiling from 84 to 82. After his age-33 season (75, played at 76) his team's view of him was about 75.3 against a cut line of 76.0 as he turned 34, about a 41% chance to stay. He survived that roll and then retired: rated below 78, his retirement chance was no longer halved, and at his age it was about one in five.

flags.text: This matches the FCS edge you were suspicious of: college level 81 going into his last year (85 by its end), then a 72-rated rookie who grew to 74 in a rotation role, with nothing in the sim to slow the step up from FCS. The call 1 first-year adjustment would decide how much that step should cost him.

Two stars at 2,225th among seniors is about right, but no FBS school offered him, while FBS signs about 850 a class from outside the top 13,800 on the scouts' upside guess alone. Real FBS staffs would offer a senior this good before those players.

label: Underrated two-star
title: Underrated two-star
story: An interior lineman who was among the top 508 of 250,000 seniors going into his senior year (level 85), he broke out from 52 to 59 that season (level 89 by its end) but got two stars and signed with FCS. After one FCS season (59 to 60) he moved up to FBS and started three years there, but only reached 65. He went undrafted (grade 68.7, ranked 569th), signed as a free agent, played one season as a backup (65 going in, 66 at the end), and was cut at 22.
why: Two stars and FCS: everyone in the top 800 on film is guaranteed three stars, so with two stars the scouts' read of his film must have put him outside the top 800, even though he ranked 508th going into his senior year, the season his film comes from. That was luck. Past that floor, stars and FBS offers lean 60 to 75% on projected upside, and his potential was only 65, so FBS passed and FCS, which signs on film, took him.

Low ceiling: an early bloomer (bloom -1.4) whose potential never rose above 67, he was within 6 points of it when he got to college at 18. He gained 1 point as an FCS starter (59 to 60) and only 5 more over three FBS seasons as a starter with coaching of 13.8.

Transfer: a lower-level player can move up through the portal if he is rated at or above the median player in his class at the level above, a slot is open and he chooses to. Most who qualify stay. At 60 after his FCS year he must have cleared that bar, and he moved up at 19.

Undrafted and cut: his 68.7 grade ranked 569th, past the 257 picks but inside the roughly 411 undrafted signings (1.6 per pick). As a backup at 65 he ended at 66 and played at 64, so his team's view of about 65.4 against a cut line of 70, with no draft protection, gave him about a 9% chance to stay.

flags.text: At 66 he was above the 65 roster mark, yet the cut line of 70 left him about a 9% chance to stay, and the cut ended his career at 22. A roster-level 22-year-old lineman would normally land on a practice squad or with another team.

He ranked 508th among seniors (level 89 by the end of his senior year) but no FBS school offered him, because offers to two-stars lean 60% on the scouts' upside guess and his potential was only 65. FBS signs about 850 a class from outside the top 13,800 instead. His two stars are the other, known problem: the scouts misread his film, as they do for about 35 of the top 500 a class, which sharper scouts in call 1 would fix.

label: True freshman who exploded
title: True freshman who exploded
story: A three-star safety who broke out as a high school senior (49 to 61, level 90 by the end of that year), he started as a true freshman at FBS and broke out again, from 61 to 71, ending that year at a college level of 90. He went into his third year at a college level of 95, left at 20 with a 79.7 grade (ranked 20th), and was taken 10th overall. He started all 16 pro seasons, reached 86 at 27 and held it through 30, and was cut at 36 after falling to 76.
why: Three stars: his film comes from the rating he played his senior season at, and going into that season he ranked 1,258th (level 82), outside the top 1,000 that four stars require on film. His breakout that year, to level 90, did not count on film. Three-stars sign with FBS first, and he landed with a strong staff (coaching 15.3).

Freshman start and breakout: college roles rank him only within his own class (about 8% start in year 1), and at 61 he made that group. Breakouts are more likely for young starters, and he got one (still partly luck), which multiplied that year's growth by 2.2 and took him from 61 to 71, playing at 74.
Draft: his third year stalled (stagnation, 76 to 76), but his 79.7 grade was far over the 70 bar to leave early. Ranked 20th, he went 10th to a front office of 8, whose board strays about 4 points.

Pro career: at 76 he started as a rookie and grew to 84 by 24 and 86 by 27. He declined from 31, and after his age-36 season (76, played at 78) his team's view of about 76.6 against a cut line of 79.6, as he turned 37, gave him about an 18% chance to stay.

flags.text: As a three-star he arrived at 61, already above the 59 median upperclass FBS starter, and started at once because roles only rank him against his own class. Real three-star freshmen rarely start, and rawer arrivals (call 1) plus depth charts (call 5) would make him earn it.

A safety who started all 16 pro seasons and was still rated 79 going into his age-36 season. Safeties usually lose their starting job in their early 30s, and 16-season safeties are rare. Decline and retirement by position are call 3.

label: Undrafted who made it
title: Undrafted who made it
story: A three-star edge rusher who was among the top 3,965 of 250,000 seniors going into his senior year (level 77), he jumped from 53 to 63 as an FBS freshman and had a breakout third year (65 to 69, played at 76, college level 84 by year end). He declared with a 70.6 grade, ranked 352nd, and went undrafted. He signed as a free agent, spent his first five pro seasons in a rotation, started three at 75 from 26 to 28, and was cut at 30 after a slump year (down from 72 to 70, played at 59).
why: Three stars and FBS: he was far outside the top 800 guaranteed three stars on film, so his three stars came from the upside side of the star score (75%), where the scouts' guess at his potential (really 72) was enough. About half of this class's three-stars come from outside the top ~5,700, so at 3,965th he was in the better half. Three-stars sign with FBS first.

College growth: in a rotation role as a freshman he gained 10 points (53 to 63), with 19 points of room under his potential of 72, as a late bloomer (bloom +0.9) with work ethic 15 and coachability 19 to take in college coaching of 12.1 (8.6 in high school). The breakout at 20 (partly luck) multiplied that year's growth by 2.2 and lifted his play to 76.

Left early, undrafted: the breakout took him to 69 and his grade came out at 70.6 (his true 69 overall and 72 potential give about 70.2), just over the 70 bar to leave after his third year. But 352nd is past the 257 picks, so he signed as one of about 411 undrafted free agents (1.6 per pick).

Pro career: with no draft protection, his team's view after year one was about 71.3 against a line of 70, only about a 66% chance to stay, so surviving was partly luck. His potential never passed 76, so he topped out at 75, and with longevity -2.4 he aged early. At 30 he ended at 70 and slumped to 59, a view of about 66.7 against a line of 72.4 as he turned 31, about a 5% chance to stay.

flags.text: He declared after his third year on a 70.6 grade that ranked 352nd, well past the 257 picks, with a year of eligibility left, and went undrafted. Leaving today rests only on the 70 bar, not on where he projects.

label: Kicker or punter
title: Kicker or punter
story: A punter who was among the top 150 of 250,000 seniors going into his senior year (level 89), he got three stars, started four years at FBS and grew from 60 to 74, ending at a college level of 90. Undrafted with a 70.6 grade (ranked 353rd), he signed as a free agent, became the starter in his second season at 76, peaked at 79 at 33, and played 18 seasons before he was cut at 39.
why: Three stars: the top 150 on film are guaranteed four stars, but kickers and punters get at most three. Three-stars sign with FBS first, and because college roles rank him only against punters in his own class, he started all four years, with coaching of 14.9.

Undrafted: kickers and punters lose 8 points on the draft grade. After his third year (73 overall, 80 potential) that gave about 68, under the 70 bar to leave early. His final 70.6 ranked 353rd, past the 257 picks, so he signed as one of about 411 undrafted free agents.

Long career: he became the starter at 23 once he reached 76 (75 is the starter mark), and was rated 75 to 79 going into every season through 38. For kickers and punters the cut line and retirement odds only start rising after 35 instead of 29 and 30, and from 28 to 34, rated 78 or better, his small retirement chance was halved.

End: from 35 on, rising cut and retirement odds gave him only about a 15% chance to still be playing at 39, so his last years were luck. After his age-39 season (73, played at 78) his team's view of about 74.5 against a cut line of 76.0, as he turned 40, gave him about a 32% chance to stay.

flags.text: He is listed as rotation as a 74-rated rookie and again at 39, but a team carries one punter, so he either punts or is not on the roster. Real position slots would fix this.

label: First-round bust
title: First-round bust
story: A three-star cornerback who was among the top 911 of 250,000 seniors going into his senior year (level 83), he started three years at FBS, grew from 56 to 70, and finished at a college level of 88. Ranked 56th on the consensus board (grade 76.5), he was taken 25th in round 1. He never reached starter level: seven pro seasons in a rotation, stuck at 74 from 25, and cut at 28.
why: Overrated by the consensus: on the grade formula his true 70 overall and 76 potential give about 72, so his 76.5 was about 4.5 points high, which was scouting error, luck. In this class a 72.4 grade ranked 206th, so graded on his true ability he would have been a late-round prospect.

Reach: a front office of 12, whose board strays about 3 points, took him 25th, 31 spots above consensus. Grades are close there (the 20th-ranked prospect graded 79.7, 3.2 above him), so a misjudgment of about 3 points in his favor, normal for that front office, could put him at the top of its board. That was luck.

Stall: an early bloomer (bloom -1.2) at cornerback, a position whose physical tools are mostly done by college, he had mainly technique and awareness left to grow. He added about a point a year (70 to 74 by 25) in a rotation role, under coaching of 11.3 to 12.3, below the pro average of 13, and stopped one point short of the 75 needed to start. His potential, 80 from 23 to 26, fell back to 76 once his growth stopped.

Cut: round-1 protection (6 points) covered his first three seasons. At 28 he ended at 74 but played at 70, so his team's view of about 72.8 against a line of 70 gave him about an 80% chance to stay. The cut was bad luck.

flags.text: He was cut at 28 while rated 74, one point below starter level, and the cut ends his career. A 74-rated corner at 28 would sign with another team in free agency, which does not exist yet.

label: Injury changed his path
title: Sixth-round receiver, nine years a starter
story: A three-star receiver, he was only among the top 5,746 of 250,000 seniors going into his senior year (level 75) but jumped from 49 to 58 that season (level 84 by its end). At FBS he went from 58 to 65 as a freshman, then had two stagnant years (66, 67) and still declared at 20, going 213th in round 6 though he ranked 272nd. He jumped to 73 as a rookie, started nine seasons from 23, peaked at 79, and was cut at 31 after a season with a major injury in which he fell from 75 to 70.
why: Three stars: going into his senior year, the season his film comes from, he ranked 5,746th, right at the edge of the class-wide finding that half of three-stars come from outside the top ~5,700. Three stars have no film requirement, so his came from the 75% weight on projected upside (his potential rose to 76 that year). By the end of that season he was at level 84, so three stars fit how he finished. Three-stars sign with FBS first, and he drew a strong staff (coaching 15.5).

Left early: two stagnation years in a row (growth x0.3) were luck. His potential of 80 still sat 13 points above his 67 rating, and at 21, his age at the draft, the grade counts about 38% of that gap, which on his true ratings comes to about 72. The consensus had him at 71.5, over the 70 bar, so he declared. Less than a point separated him from the 206th-ranked prospect (72.4), and a front office of 13, whose board strays about 2.75 points, took him 213th.

Rookie jump: the stagnant years left him 13 points under his potential, and as a late bloomer (bloom +0.7) he was still in his growth window, so normal growth came back: 67 to 73 as a rookie and 75 by 22, enough to start at 23.

End: with longevity -1.2 he aged early, slipping from 79 at 27 to 75 at 30. A major injury at 31 (it takes explosiveness and ceiling) came in the year he dropped to 70 and his potential from 76 to 71. His team's view of about 70 against a line of 73.6, as he turned 32, gave him about a 14% chance to stay.

flags.text: He left after his third year coming off two stagnant seasons, with a grade that ranked 272nd, outside the 257 picks, and a year of eligibility left. Today the only test is the 70 bar, and call 2 would weigh his projection and his flat final year.

label: Random draft pick
title: Four-star interior lineman, 14 years a starter
story: An interior lineman who was among the top 357 of 250,000 seniors going into his senior year (level 86), he got four stars, started at FBS as a true freshman and jumped from 63 to 74, reaching a college level of 95 by his third year. He left at 20 with an 83.3 grade (ranked 6th) and went 16th overall. He started all 14 pro seasons, sat at 85 or 86 from 26 on, and retired after his age-34 season still rated 85.
why: Four stars: going into his senior year he ranked 357th, inside the top 1,000 that four stars require on film but outside the top 150 guaranteed them, so the star score, 75% projected upside, did the rest (his potential was 81). He signed with FBS and drew a top staff (coaching 18.8, above the 15 average even for the very top recruits, so partly luck).

Freshman jump: college roles rank him only within his own class (about 8% start in year 1), and at 63 he made that group. As a starter (growth x1.15) with work ethic 15 (x1.125), coaching of 18.8 (though coachability 6 limits how much sticks) and 18 points of room under his potential, he went from 63 to 74.

Draft: his 83.3 grade was far over the 70 bar, so he left after his third year. Ranked 6th, he slid to 16th because the 32 teams pick off their own boards, which stray about 1 to 6 points depending on the front office, and a front office of 12 (about 3 points) took him.

Pro career: a starter from day one at 78, he reached 83 by 22. Lost seasons at 23 and 26 (growth x0.4, more likely with competitiveness 6) slowed him, and a lost season also pulls potential down: his slipped from 87 to 86 that year and 85 by 24, and he settled at 85 to 86. Players rated 85 and up retire a quarter as often, so retiring after his age-34 season was about a 6% chance: luck.

flags.text: An interior lineman arrived at college at 63, above the 59 median upperclass FBS starter, and was a 92-level college player after one year. Linemen are meant to arrive rawer than skill players, and true-freshman interior starters are rare, so rawer arrivals would make this less common.

label: Random draft pick

why: Five stars fit: five-stars come only from the top 100 on film, and he was one of only 32 seniors at level 93 or above, so his stars followed real high school ability.

Little college growth: as a receiver and an early bloomer (bloom -2.5), most of his physical growth was done before college. A freshman slump (he played at 62 on a 67 rating) cut that year's growth and cost a little skill. His body stalled at 19, capping his physical ceilings for good, the year his potential slipped from 81 to 79. Even strong coaching of 18.4 (his coachability of 8, a little below average, means slightly less of it sticks) got him only from 67 to 72 in three years.

Left after three years and went near his spot: after a third year any grade of 70 or more makes a player declare, and his was 78.2. His real 72 overall and 80 potential work out to about 75, so the scouts read him about 3 points high, which was luck. He ranked 35th, and a front office of 13 (misjudgment about 2.75 points) took him 37th, close to the consensus.

Cut: a slump (which also takes a little skill) left him at 72 under pro coaching of 9.9, below the pro average of 13, and he played at 66. His team's view of him was about 70.2 against a cut line of 66 after round-2 protection, about an 89% chance to stay, so the cut was bad luck.

flags.text: The 37th pick, 21 years old, rated 72 with potential 80, was cut after one season and is out of football for good. Real teams almost never cut a second-rounder after one year, and if one did, another team would sign him. This class cuts 4 to 7 of its 64 first- and second-rounders within two seasons.

label: Random FBS or FCS player

With that, work ethic 17, late blooming (bloom 1.1) and a redshirt year's extra physical growth, he went from 47 to 53 in his first year and to 63 by the end, and his potential rose from 61 to 70.

Slow start: he was a backup at 19 and had a lost season (he played at 47 and grew only 1 point). That was bad luck, since his work ethic of 17 makes a lost season less likely than for most players. Roles go by rank within his own class and the share who start rises each year, so he moved up to rotation at 20 and starter at 21.

Undrafted and unsigned: his grade never reached 70, so he stayed all five years. His final 66 ranked 974th, well past the 257 picks and the roughly 410 undrafted signings (about 1.6 per pick), and at 63 overall he was below the 65 roster level.
